article.title: DoltLite Reaches Beta, Bringing Git-Style Branching and Cloning to a SQLite Fork Built From 2,000 AI Agent Pull Requests
article.summary: DoltHub's DoltLite, a SQLite fork with Dolt-style version control, hit Beta five months after launch, built with about 2,000 agent-generated pull requests.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

DoltLite, a fork of SQLite that adds Git-style version control, has reached Beta as version 0.50.0, according to a [DoltHub blog post](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-08-31-doltlite-beta/) by Tim Sehn published August 31, 2026. The [GitHub release page](https://github.com/dolthub/doltlite/releases/tag/v0.50.0) records the tag as going live at 19:37 UTC that day. The Beta arrives five months after DoltLite's initial [alpha launch on March 25, 2026](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-03-25-doltlite/), according to DoltHub.

## What We Know

DoltLite is built by replacing SQLite's B-tree storage layer with a Prolly Tree — a content-addressed B-tree — backed by a single file chunk store, while leaving SQLite's SQL parser, analyzer, file-system interaction layer, and test harness untouched, according to [DoltHub](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-08-31-doltlite-beta/). Prolly Trees are the same data structure that powers version control across DoltHub's other products, the company said. The result is a SQLite-compatible embedded database that supports branching, merging, and diffing, plus Git-style remote operations — push, pull, clone, and fetch — either against a custom remote or against DoltHub itself, per the blog post.

According to DoltHub, the project began as a test case for Steve Yegge's agent orchestrator, Gas Town, after the company had wanted an embedded version of its Dolt database for years but considered rewriting Dolt's storage engine in C or Rust impractical. Building DoltLite on top of SQLite instead took about 2,000 pull requests, according to the [DoltHub blog post](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-08-31-doltlite-beta/). At its March 2026 launch, DoltLite's storage engine and version-control additions amounted to roughly 18,000 lines of new C code, with only eight lines of the original SQLite C code changed, and the DoltLite-specific code was licensed Apache 2.0 while SQLite's own source remained public domain, DoltHub said in the [launch post](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-03-25-doltlite/). At launch, DoltHub described the project as being in alpha and "entirely vibe-coded using Gas Town."

DoltHub frames the Beta designation around four commitments: storage format stability, SQL compatibility, full version control, and production performance. On format stability, the company said it took 12 backward-incompatible storage format changes to reach Beta, and that DoltLite has now been on its current format for 57 releases, spanning more than three months of calendar time, according to the [blog post](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-08-31-doltlite-beta/). On SQL compatibility, DoltHub said DoltLite passes 100% of sqllogictest, a suite of 5.8 million complex queries, and 99.46% of SQLite's own 892,277 TCL-based acceptance tests, with 4,809 known divergences. The company attributed most of those divergences to three causes: DoltLite keys tables by primary key rather than rowid to support version control, and some tests inspect rowid directly; DoltLite organizes storage into chunks rather than pages, and some tests inspect pages directly; and DoltLite has no write-ahead-log or journal sidecar, so WAL and journal tests are skipped, per the blog post.

On version control, DoltHub said DoltLite supports local operations including branches, merges, diffs, rebases, cherry-picks, and resets, along with remote push, pull, clone, and fetch, and ships with the full Dolt Workbench GUI, including an "agent mode" that lets a coding agent run `dolt_reset('--hard')` to undo changes it made to a database, according to the [blog post](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-08-31-doltlite-beta/).

On performance, DoltHub publishes a nightly sysbench-style benchmark on GitHub comparing DoltLite against stock SQLite. Per the [August 31 blog post](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-08-31-doltlite-beta/), the most recent report at the time of publication showed in-memory DoltLite databases running 10% slower than SQLite on reads and 60% slower on writes, while file-backed databases were at parity on reads and 10% slower on batched writes. The largest gap was on small autocommit writes, which DoltHub measured at 3.1 times slower than SQLite — about 400 microseconds per write in DoltLite versus about 125 microseconds in SQLite, measured on what the company called "a tiny GitHub runner." DoltHub recommends batching writes where performance matters.

## What We Don't Know

DoltHub's blog post does not disclose how many organizations or projects have adopted DoltLite in production, nor does it name specific production users. The company also has not stated whether or when DoltLite will move from Sehn's personal GitHub account into the main DoltHub GitHub organization, a transition the [March launch post](https://www.dolthub.com/blog/2026-03-25-doltlite/) said would depend on usage and interest.

## Analysis

DoltLite's SQL-compatibility numbers are a direct consequence of its architecture: because the SQL parser, analyzer, and test harness are unmodified SQLite code, and only the storage layer beneath them was replaced, the project inherits SQLite's existing test suites almost wholesale rather than having to prove compatibility from scratch — a different validation path than Dolt itself took when it built a version-controlled SQL engine from the ground up, according to DoltHub's own account of the project's origins.
